Ranked differential (most to least likely) with brief rationale and key confirming tests

1) Localized scleroderma (morphea profunda / linear or "en plaque" deep morphea)
   - Rationale: Unilateral, long‑standing, slowly progressive stony‑hard plaque in a child with skin hyperpigmentation, loss of elasticity, hypertrichosis and progressive joint restriction — classic for deep morphea affecting dermis/subcutis/fascia.
   - Confirmation: Deep skin/fascia biopsy showing thickened collagen bundles with loss of adnexal structures and perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate; MRI showing fascial/subcutaneous involvement; possible positive ANA.

2) Eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman syndrome)
   - Rationale: Can cause indurated, woody plaques with fascial involvement and joint contracture; may present with peripheral eosinophilia and raised inflammatory markers. Less common in children and typically more abrupt.
   - Confirmation: Biopsy showing fascial thickening with eosinophils; MRI with fascial enhancement; peripheral eosinophilia/↑ESR.

3) Fibrous hamartoma of childhood / fibromatosis (benign fibrous tumor)
   - Rationale: Firm subcutaneous or intramuscular fibrous mass presenting in childhood; may be slowly progressive and produce overlying skin changes and restricted movement.
   - Confirmation: Biopsy with characteristic histologic pattern of fibrous tissue and immature mesenchymal elements; MRI showing a localized mass.

4) Chronic panniculitis / lupus panniculitis or post‑inflammatory fibrosis
   - Rationale: Chronic inflammation of subcutis can produce indurated, hyperpigmented plaques and scarring; less typical age/presentation but possible.
   - Confirmation: Biopsy showing lobular panniculitis with characteristic inflammatory infiltrate or fat necrosis; serology (ANA, complement) if lupus suspected.

5) Panniculitis‑like cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma or other neoplasm (rare)
   - Rationale: Rare cause of progressive indurated plaques; should be considered when lesions are atypical or biopsy shows atypical lymphoid infiltrate.
   - Confirmation: Biopsy with atypical lymphoid cells and T‑cell receptor studies/immunophenotyping.

Plan and next steps
- Proceed with the requested MRI and full‑thickness biopsy as priority to differentiate deep morphea from eosinophilic fasciitis and neoplasm; blood tests will support inflammatory/autoimmune or eosinophilic processes.
- Once results are available (MRI + histopathology ± bloods), I will give a definitive diagnosis and recommend appropriate treatment (e.g., topical/systemic immunomodulation, physiotherapy, or surgical options if a mass).
